questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Particle Is at Instantaneous Rest
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $3{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $2\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/52d095f73fdaa91c6a2fe9f2caca74929a22ec09618e85395732ea451bda81c7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $3{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-3{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-3{x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =-(2)^{3}+C \\ C & =2+8 \\ C & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=10-{x}^{3}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =10-{x}^{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =10-{x}^{3} \\ {x}^{3} & =10 \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{10}\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $9{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $4\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\sqrt[3]{3}\,m,$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/cefc91f25690470124503ab4da79245a95896ecc71f562d9a268d9f79ce0de58.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $9{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=9{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=9{x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=3{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=\sqrt[3]{3}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =3{(\sqrt[3]{3})}^{3}+C \\ 8 & =9+C \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=3{x}^{3}-1.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =3{x}^{3}-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =3{x}^{3}-1 \\ 3{x}^{3}-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =\frac{1}{3} \\ x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{3}}\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is ${x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $2\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\sqrt[3]{7}\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/1b474c320ec59107dd191ab4420f0d4edb1e551164d90b741338da1e0dd3b23d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=\sqrt[3]{7}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt[3]{7})^{3}+C \\ C & =2-\frac{7}{3} \\ C & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{{x}^{3}-1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{{x}^{3}-1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =\frac{{x}^{3}-1}{3} \\ {x}^{3}-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =1 \\ x & =1\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $6{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $2\sqrt{7}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/a8c9778580276589ff7a047ca3c7b620de842efd7b3799a70b6e4484bc5fa0e6.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\sqrt{7}\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{7})^{2} & =-2(1)^{3}+C \\ C & =14+2 \\ C & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=16-2{x}^{3}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =16-2{x}^{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =16-2{x}^{3} \\ 2{x}^{3} & =16 \\ {x}^{3} & =8 \\ x & =2\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x\ge \frac{1}{2}.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $1\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/cdb88c0c679ca9325df42c5c8c4feaea6ce6c0cf02655410158860d7b03d54dc.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-(4x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-(4x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-4x+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=1\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =-2{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+2(\frac{1}{2})+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-1 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ 2x(1-x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x\ge \frac{1}{2}$ is $x=1\,m.$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(k-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/6f34d18ec0aed1f28e77a143c5be0b3d4eaf44ba08649d02517c6c6ea5bc0af4.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(k-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k-x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (k-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(0)-\frac{(0)^{2}}{2}+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+8.
$$

Finally, since $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(2)-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+8 \\ 12 & =2k+6 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $kx\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=20\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $10\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/cd42eb74e5bba02951118c349a1b25f7193c39aa53f6504403918dfa984eb2c2.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $kx\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-kx)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=20\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(20)^{2} & =-\frac{k}{2}(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =200\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=200-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,m/s$ when $x=10\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =200-\frac{k}{2}{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =200-\frac{k}{2}(10)^{2} \\ 50k & =200 \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of the acceleration is $k{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant, and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=16\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle is at rest when its displacement is $20\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/4c997edf5c34a22fc71eac697c161434797c938df40760ae1089fd6e62db795d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $k{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-k{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-k{x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-k{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-\frac{k}{3}{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=16\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-\frac{k}{3}{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(16)^{2} & =-\frac{k}{3}(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =128\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=128-\frac{k}{3}{x}^{3}.
$$

Finally, since $v=0\,{m/s}^{2}$ when $x=20\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =128-\frac{k}{3}{x}^{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =128-\frac{k}{3}(20)^{3} \\ \frac{8,000k}{3} & =128 \\ 8,000k & =384 \\ k & =\frac{6}{125}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the positive $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k\sqrt{x}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=6\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $9\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/b052a65fb0dbcc14a5d359b693beafdf5da3f4bbe1e10f006c315e8168340d5c.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k\sqrt{x}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k\sqrt{x}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k\sqrt{x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (k\sqrt{x})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}(0)^{3/2}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+18.
$$

Finally, since $v=6\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=9\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}{x}^{3/2}+18 \\ \frac{1}{2}(6\sqrt{6})^{2} & =\frac{2k}{3}(9)^{3/2}+18 \\ 108 & =18k+18 \\ 18k & =90 \\ k & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(10-2x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/33b95a6985a53b76eb7f74771825c18f21d1e59b2245325e14690a365a2a8bb0.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(10-2x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=10-2x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10-2x & =0 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=5\,m.$

canonical_examples.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x \geq 1.$  When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(2x-2) \, \rm{m/s}^2,$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $\sqrt2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1\,\rm{m},$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/0c47a1e988a75e4813c92a76acbf3a821364995123f3eb394b07d4bfaa95f80d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(2x-2)\,\rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -(2x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -(2x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x
=
\int (-2x+2) \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x + C.
$$

Now, since $v=\sqrt{2}\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=1\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2})^{2} & =-(1)^{2}+2(1)+C \\ C & =1+1-2 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = -x^2+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-{x}^{2}+2x \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x \geq 1$ is $x=2\,\rm{m}.$

If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=4\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1 \,\rm{m},$ find the value of $k.$

\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(5x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(5(1)-\frac{1}{2}{(1)}^{2})+3 \\ 12 & =\frac{9k}{2}+3 \\ \frac{9k}{2} & =9 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2(5x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+3 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =10x-{x}^{2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =20x-2{x}^{2}+6 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+20x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \sqrt{-2x^2 + 20x + 6}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
v_{\max} = v(5) =\sqrt{-2(5)^2 + 20(5) + 6} = 2\sqrt{14}\,\rm{m/s}
$$
